title: Foundations of Nursing Practice: Pain, Sleep & Comfort
html:
Comfort is more than a low pain score. It includes the client's ability to breathe deeply, move, rest, eat, participate in care, and feel safe and respected. The RN treats pain as the client's personal experience, gathers a complete assessment, uses prescribed and appropriate comfort measures, and evaluates whether the plan supports the function that matters to the client.

Learning goals

  • Perform a focused, respectful pain assessment using the client's report and observable cues.
  • Set a realistic comfort-function goal with the client.
  • Use prescribed pharmacologic and appropriate nonpharmacologic comfort measures safely.
  • Support restorative sleep and reduce avoidable disruption.
  • Recognize pain or sedation changes that need timely escalation.

Assess pain as a multidimensional experience

Ask about location, intensity, quality, onset, timing, what makes the pain better or worse, associated symptoms, previous strategies, and the effect on activity, sleep, appetite, mood, and concentration. PQRSTU is one structured approach: provocation or palliation, quality, region or radiation, severity, timing, and understanding of the problem. Respect the client's report; a calm appearance or a communication barrier does not prove absence of pain.

For clients who cannot provide a self-report, use the facility-approved observational tool and compare behavioral cues such as guarding, grimacing, moaning, restlessness, or withdrawal with baseline. Ask family or caregivers about the client's usual pain behaviors when appropriate. Objective cues inform assessment but do not replace individualized evaluation.

Urgent pain cue
New severe pain, chest pressure or pain, pain with instability, or pain that changes suddenly from baseline needs immediate focused assessment and the required escalation. Do not simply repeat a routine comfort measure and wait.

Plan for comfort and function

Ask what the client needs to be able to do: cough, take a deep breath, sleep, walk to the bathroom, participate in therapy, or sit with family. A comfort-function goal is more useful than a number alone. Positioning, splinting, a calm environment, heat or cold when ordered and appropriate, relaxation, breathing techniques, music, distraction, hygiene, and supportive communication can complement—not replace—the prescribed plan.

Before an anticipated painful activity, review the plan, timing, and safety needs. Do not administer a medication, apply heat or cold, or use another treatment outside the order, contraindications, and facility policy. Clients with new pain need assessment, not an assumption that their existing plan is still appropriate.

Medication safety and reassessment

Verify the medication order, allergy history, indication, baseline pain assessment, vital signs, level of sedation, respiratory status, and relevant precautions before giving an analgesic. Follow the required timing for reassessment based on the medication, route, onset, and policy. After any intervention, assess both relief and adverse effects, including excessive sedation or respiratory change when relevant. If the client is not meeting the comfort-function goal or develops concerning effects, follow the escalation process rather than independently changing the dose or schedule.

Protect sleep and rest

Start with an open question such as “Do you feel rested when you wake up?” Ask about the usual routine, naps, pain, anxiety, noise, light, temperature, breathing symptoms, devices, and nighttime interruptions. In the hospital, rest can be disrupted by illness, alarms, uncomfortable positioning, pain, care activities, and an unfamiliar environment. Collaborate to cluster nonurgent care when safe, reduce light and noise, offer hygiene and comfort measures, support the bedtime routine when possible, and schedule pain treatment according to the plan.

Do not label sleep loss as noncompliance or simply add a sedating medication without assessment. Increasing daytime sleepiness, new confusion, breathing concerns at night, or a persistent pattern of poor rest merits evaluation and communication.

Evaluate the response

Reassess the client-defined goal, pain characteristics, ability to function, sleep quality, adverse effects, vital signs as indicated, level of sedation, and the client's satisfaction with the plan. Document the intervention and response objectively. A plan is successful when it improves safe function and rest at a level meaningful to the client—not only when a single score changes.

Clinical example

A postoperative client says the incision pain is 7/10 and declines to cough because of fear of pain. The RN assesses the pain using PQRSTU, reviews sedation and respiratory status, confirms the prescribed plan, collaborates on a goal of coughing with manageable discomfort, provides the ordered intervention and splinting education, then reassesses pain, respiratory status, and ability to cough. The follow-up shows whether the intervention supported recovery.
